## Foundations: Mindset, Bankroll and Journaling
Source: https://trading-study-notes.sanliurfa.workers.dev/notes/A_foundations

# Foundations: Mindset, Bankroll and Journaling

*Original study notes. All prose here is written from scratch; the linked videos are the original sources and remain their authors' property. Click any timestamp to open that moment in the source video.*

## 1. Trading as a game against yourself

The starting idea is that the market is an arena in which the main opponent is the trader. Outcomes are uncertain, so the useful question is not "will this win?" but "did I make a good decision under uncertainty?" Most participants are expected to lose, and the way to avoid that group is not a secret indicator but better decisions and better money management.

A second framing is that this is gambling analysis. Nobody knows the next price. Each setup is like a door leading to a different possible future, and once price has moved through a door, that branch is closed. The trader's job is to estimate which branches are more likely, act on that estimate, and manage the downside when reality takes another path.

Effort, not account size, drives improvement. Depositing more money does not make a trader better; deliberate practice does. The early months are for learning with small size, not for searching for a 100x.

Sources: *Lesson 1 — Introduction to Trading* ([00:04], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LKJPwG14y2M); ([04:30], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LKJPwG14y2M); *Becoming a Trader Part 1* ([00:04], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MCqrvhZmrdA).

## 2. Start small and learn your own statistics

The first account should be deliberately small — tens or hundreds of units rather than thousands. The reason is practical: you cannot learn position sizing, emotional control, or win rate from a size you are afraid to lose. A useful test is whether you can turn a very small stake into several times its size before adding capital; if you cannot do it small, adding size usually magnifies the same mistakes.

Win rate must be measured, not assumed. Knowing that a trade won is not enough; you need to know why it won, what the average win and average loss look like, and how the number was produced. A trader who cannot state their own average bet size has a capital-management problem before they have a strategy problem.

The blow-up pattern is well known: a lucky run turns a small account into a large one, a few careless trades give most of it back, and the trader re-deposits expecting the market to "owe" them. Avoiding that arc matters more than finding the next entry.

Sources: *Becoming a Trader Part 1* ([03:55], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MCqrvhZmrdA); ([07:10], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MCqrvhZmrdA); *Becoming a Trader Part 2 — Bankroll Management* ([02:33], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0LFo5f1TtHA).

## 3. Data on yourself: journal and diary

Two separate records are recommended.

**Trading journal.** A log of the trades themselves: entry, stop, target, size, reason for the trade, what happened, and what was learned. A 90-day challenge is suggested as a starting block, then another, and then the practice continues indefinitely. The journal tells you whether the rules are being followed.

**Trading diary.** A record of the trader, not the trades: mood, energy, sleep, hours worked, day of week, emotional state at the time of the decision. The purpose is to find recurring leaks. If losses cluster on certain days or in certain moods, that pattern is more actionable than another chart pattern.

Decisions can be mapped as decision trees. For each situation, list the possible responses and the likely emotional consequence. The aim is to identify the specific choices that lead to an unhappy outcome and remove them one by one, rather than trying to fix everything at once.

Sources: *Becoming a Trader Part 1* ([04:36], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MCqrvhZmrdA); ([09:09], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MCqrvhZmrdA); ([12:40], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MCqrvhZmrdA); *The Key to Success* ([18:36], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UfxEboq-tOM).

## 4. Bankroll rules

- Keep bet size constant. Changing size after a win or loss is how a good process turns into gambling.
- Use a separate, untouchable long-term holding portfolio and a dedicated trading portfolio. Mixing them leads to risking money that was meant to be safe.
- Avoid "full stack" swings. Putting the entire trading account on one outcome is comparable to high leverage even when no leverage is used.
- Do not over-diversify. A small number of well-understood positions is preferred over dozens of coins the trader cannot follow.
- The poker reference point: at a $1/$2 cash game, a serious bankroll is around $20,000, so a $200 loss is a small fraction. The same proportional thinking applies to trading size.
- A personal martingale variant is described in the source material but explicitly presented as an experiment, not a recommendation.

Sources: *Becoming a Trader Part 2* ([03:45], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0LFo5f1TtHA); ([08:22], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0LFo5f1TtHA); *Things You Should Not Do in 2025* ([05:05], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mPMn_g20SHU).

## 5. Leverage and position size

Leverage is treated as a money-management choice rather than a strategy. Ten times leverage on a large account and one hundred times leverage on a small account can control the same notional exposure; what changes is how much room the position has before liquidation and how the trader feels about the number on screen.

The psychological ceiling on size is real. Scaling from tiny trades to large ones changes decision quality. Increase size only after the smaller size has been handled consistently, and keep the step small enough that a losing streak does not change behaviour.

Sources: *Introduction — New to This YouTube?* ([04:14], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JKLiG3p-qN4); *Basic Explanation of EMAs Part 1* ([30:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5hiv8vzMxcA).

## 6. Keeping the money

Making money and keeping it are different skills. The rule is that profit taken from a trade should be moved out of the exchange and into a wallet the trader controls, rather than recycled into the next position. Withdrawal discipline is what converts a good run into a lasting result.

Daily goals should be concrete and achievable. If the day's target is a modest amount, take the profit when it appears instead of holding out for more and watching the trade turn into a loss. A completed small target beats an open-ended hope.

Sources: *Introduction — New to This YouTube?* ([08:32], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JKLiG3p-qN4); *Becoming a Trader Part 3 — Defining Your Goals* ([05:46], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zGUhlJOtQM8).

## 7. Rules, checklists and planning

The best traders cited in the material all work from written rules — not only exit and stop rules, but rules about when to trade, when to stop for the day, and how many attempts to make. A checklist turns those rules into something repeatable under stress.

Trades should be planned before entry: the invalidation level, the target area, the size, and the story for why the setup exists. The phrase used in the sources is to write the story rather than react to the story. If the story changes after entry without a structural reason, that is usually a sign to exit rather than to justify holding.

A three-strike convention appears in the lessons: after a small number of failed attempts in a session, stop and come back later. The point is to prevent tilted, repeated entries from turning a small loss into a large one.

Sources: *The Key to Success* ([19:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UfxEboq-tOM); *Becoming a Trader Part 5 — Planning Your Trades* ([07:25], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nbVJwTkwZ5w); *Lesson 4 — Starting Trading from Scratch* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pZOQbD_7UAc).

## 8. Learning routine

Ask specific questions. Instead of "is this a good trade?", ask what would invalidate the idea, which timeframe is being traded, and what the higher timeframe says. Verify claims against the source video rather than memory — that is what the timestamp links are for.

The training horizon is measured in months, not days. Practice across different market regimes, because a trader who only sees a bear market or only a bull market will be unprepared when the character of the market changes. Adaptability is treated as a core skill: being willing to be wrong about a read is what allows the read to be corrected.

Sources: *The Basic of TA — Setting Up Charts* ([35:09], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY); *Becoming a Trader Part 4 — Mastering Yourself* ([02:02], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gJNO11fkK_Y).

## Mistakes, Anti-Patterns and Risk
Source: https://trading-study-notes.sanliurfa.workers.dev/notes/B_mistakes

# Mistakes, Anti-Patterns and Risk

*Original study notes. The linked videos are the original sources and remain their authors' property. Click a timestamp to jump to the relevant moment.*

## 1. The common failure patterns

Most losses can be traced to a short list of behaviours rather than to a missing indicator: trading too large, trading too often, refusing to take profit, moving stops, and treating a lucky outcome as skill. The cure is unglamorous — know your limit, stay inside it, and collect data on yourself until the patterns are visible.

The classic blow-up sequence is a strong run that inflates confidence, a period of careless sizing, a deep drawdown, and then a re-deposit made with the feeling that the market will eventually turn. Recognising the sequence early is more useful than predicting the market itself.

Sources: *Things You Should Not Do in 2025* ([05:05], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mPMn_g20SHU); *Do Not Make These Mistakes Trading in 2026* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CXwXDa-9YCs).

## 2. Bankroll and concentration

Start with an amount whose loss would not change your behaviour. If a small stake cannot be grown, a larger one will not fix the underlying problem. Keep bet size constant; changing size after a win or a loss is one of the fastest ways to turn a process into a gamble.

Avoid using the whole account on a single idea. Full-size swings carry the same practical risk as high leverage, even without leverage. Over-diversification is the opposite error: holding dozens of coins makes it impossible to follow any of them. A handful of instruments that you know well is preferred.

Sources: *Things You Should Not Do in 2025* ([05:05], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mPMn_g20SHU); *The Basic of TA — Setting Up Charts* ([38:36], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY).

## 3. Accept that it is gambling

The source material is explicit: an entry is a bet on an unknown outcome. Calling it an investment or a profession does not change that. What can be improved is the quality of the bet — the size, the invalidation, the target, and the decision process — not the certainty of the result.

Sources: *Lesson 1 — Introduction to Trading* ([03:31], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LKJPwG14y2M); *Things You Should Not Do in 2025* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mPMn_g20SHU).

## 4. Taking profit

A winning position that becomes a losing one is a self-inflicted error. The recommended habit is to close part of a trade once it is in profit rather than waiting for a perfect exit. A partial close of roughly 60–70% is described as a reasonable default; 50% is more aggressive. Once part has been banked, the remaining position can be given a wider stop, because it is being carried by the result rather than by hope.

Do not be angry about taking profit. There will be another trade. If a trade is closed too early, the response is to plan the partial close in advance next time, not to replay the decision emotionally.

Sources: *Lesson 3 — Trade Strategy* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8WAUnwtRBE8); *Lesson 5 — Leverage, Taking Profit, Thinking Ahead* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UscLoywpZR0); *Key Thoughts Going Into 2026* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ti3JhXEY9UM).

## 5. Happy decisions and emotional leaks

The practical test for a decision is whether it leaves you calm. Trades opened out of boredom, revenge, or fear tend to share identifiable features — a familiar coin, a familiar time of day, a familiar mood. Find those recurring situations in the diary and remove them one at a time.

The trader controls the button. No chart, indicator, or commenter places the order. Framing decisions as choices you own makes it easier to accept both good and bad outcomes as information rather than as verdicts on your worth.

Sources: *Mastering Yourself* ([01:10], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gJNO11fkK_Y); *Do Not Make These Mistakes Trading in 2026* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CXwXDa-9YCs).

## 6. Stop losses as invalidation

A stop is not a dollar amount you are willing to lose; it is the price at which the reason for the trade stops being true. Placing it by account size rather than by chart structure is the most common mistake.

Use recent swing wicks and key areas to decide where the idea breaks. If price moves above a wick that marked a rejection, the thesis is wrong and the exit is justified even if the loss feels large. Conversely, if the structure is intact, a stop placed only to soothe emotion is likely to be hit and reversed.

Sources: *Guide to Stop Losses — Introduction* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yNhmxEc6y5c); *Key Thoughts Going Into 2026* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ti3JhXEY9UM).

## 7. Liquidity and stop hunting

Market makers push price toward obvious clusters of stops. Horizontal levels that everyone can see attract price, which is why stops placed just beyond a well-marked level are often swept before the move continues. Draw the level, but expect the wick through it.

Sources: *Do Not Make These Mistakes Trading in 2026* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CXwXDa-9YCs); *How to Use Aggr.Trade (2025)* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KPD2ElzbQnc).

## 8. Entry timing and overtrading

Entering late is a recurring error: the trade is opened after the move has already happened, which leaves no room for the stop. Wait for the pullback or the confirmation the story requires.

Set a daily limit on attempts. Three unsuccessful entries in a session is a common stopping point. Continuing beyond that is usually an emotional decision rather than a technical one.

Sources: *Part 1 — Timing Your Positions* ([04:48], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NyGIkmMb-Sw); *Lesson 3 — Trade Strategy* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8WAUnwtRBE8).

## 9. Keep the toolkit small

A recurring warning is against indicator collecting. The core toolkit is RSI, stochastic RSI, a few EMAs, Ichimoku, and Keltner/Watson levels — used together to tell one coherent story. Adding more tools usually adds more excuses, not more edge. The three-minute chart in particular is overused; higher timeframes provide the context that makes a lower-timeframe entry meaningful.

Sources: *Lesson Number 5 — Stochastic RSI and Keltner Channels* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7MmCcxadAwQ); *How to Approach Timeframe* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VoIr0w6l8gc).

## 10. Study, security and adaptability

Journal the reason for every decision, including the ones you are unsure about. Do not copy another trader's entries without understanding the invalidation; a copied position cannot be managed when the story changes. Keep exchange balances low and hold long-term assets in self-custody.

Finally, stay willing to be wrong about a market view. The willingness to update a thesis is what separates a flexible trader from one who keeps forcing an outdated story onto new price action.

Sources: *The Key to Success* ([18:08], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UfxEboq-tOM); *Key Thoughts Going Into 2026* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ti3JhXEY9UM).

## Trading Lessons and Philosophy
Source: https://trading-study-notes.sanliurfa.workers.dev/notes/C_lessons

# Trading Lessons and Philosophy

*Original study notes. The linked videos are the original sources and remain their authors' property. Click any timestamp to open the exact moment.*

## 1. The reality of the game

Trading is presented as an activity where making money is easier than keeping it. A correct guess is common; repeated correct decisions with controlled size are not. The metaphor used in the lessons is a set of doors: every setup opens several possible futures, and price closes some of them as it moves. A good trade is one where the chosen branch was more likely and the downside was defined before entry.

Two characters are contrasted. One style takes profits, keeps them, and moves on. The other holds for more, gives the gain back, and then trades emotionally to recover it. The difference is behaviour, not analysis.

Sources: *Lesson 1 — Introduction to Trading* ([00:04], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LKJPwG14y2M); ([04:30], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LKJPwG14y2M); ([13:34], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LKJPwG14y2M).

## 2. Where the edge comes from

Concentration is the central theme. Pick one major coin — the material suggests one of the larger names — and learn its behaviour across timeframes. Knowing one instrument's rhythm, volume patterns, and key areas is treated as more valuable than shallow knowledge of twenty.

Other sources of edge listed in the lessons:

- Recognising recurring patterns rather than predicting a single outcome.
- Reading market emotion and energy: where participants feel strongly, price tends to react.
- Understanding how the chosen exchange behaves, including its funding and liquidation mechanics.
- Treating Bitcoin dominance as context for the rest of the market.

Sources: *Lesson 2 — Alpha That Will Save You Thousands* ([28:41], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rLdY77E8KzA); *The Basic of TA — Setting Up Charts* ([29:56], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY).

## 3. The happy decision

A decision is judged by whether it can be lived with calmly. "Happy trading" in these notes means not focusing on the money while the trade is open: the entry, invalidation, and target were decided earlier, so the only remaining job is to follow them. A trade that produces anxiety was probably mis-sized or poorly planned.

Sources: *Lesson 3 — Trade Strategy* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8WAUnwtRBE8); *Mastering Yourself* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gJNO11fkK_Y).

## 4. Rules and discipline

Written rules cover entries, exits, size, daily limits, and when to stop for the day. They are useful precisely because they were written when calm and are followed when the market is not. A checklist converts them into a repeatable pre-trade routine.

The three-strike convention appears across the lessons: if the first few setups fail, stop rather than forcing a fourth. A constant bet size is part of the same discipline — no doubling after a loss and no size increase after a win.

Sources: *The Key to Success* ([19:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UfxEboq-tOM); *Lesson 3 — Trade Strategy* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8WAUnwtRBE8).

## 5. Stops and invalidation

A stop loss marks where the idea is wrong, not how much money the trader is prepared to lose. Place it at a structural level — a recent wick, a range boundary, an EMA on the relevant timeframe — and accept that a sweep of obvious stops is part of the game. Moving a stop further away to avoid taking a loss converts a defined trade into an open-ended bet.

Sources: *Guide to Stop Losses — Introduction* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yNhmxEc6y5c); *Key Thoughts Going Into 2026* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ti3JhXEY9UM).

## 6. Taking profit and adding back

Partial closes are planned in advance. A common pattern is to bank a substantial part of the move, then let the remainder run with a wider stop. Adding back is only discussed in the context of a trade already in profit and with a new invalidation level; adding to a losing position is not part of the method.

The warning against turning a winner into a loser is repeated often. A small, certain gain is preferred to a larger possible gain that requires perfect timing.

Sources: *Lesson 5 — Leverage, Taking Profit, Thinking Ahead* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UscLoywpZR0); *Lesson 4 — Starting Trading from Scratch* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pZOQbD_7UAc).

## 7. Leverage

Leverage changes the room a position has, not the quality of the idea. The material compares high leverage on a small account with low leverage on a large one: the notional exposure can be identical. What matters is whether the stop fits inside the price noise and whether the trader can follow the plan without panic.

Sources: *Lesson 5 — Leverage, Taking Profit, Thinking Ahead* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UscLoywpZR0); *Basic Explanation of EMAs Part 1* ([30:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5hiv8vzMxcA).

## 8. Shorting

Shorting is treated as a separate skill with its own mindset. The examples emphasise waiting for confirmation on the higher timeframe, placing the stop above a structural level, and taking partial profit into downward moves. The same rule applies: a short opened without an invalidation level is a bet, not a trade.

Sources: *The Art of Shorting — Part 1* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-RFNrX5GNoc).

## 9. The chart toolkit

The tools used together are:

- Horizontal levels drawn at high-volume areas, extended forward rather than erased.
- RSI read with health levels rather than fixed 70/30 rules.
- Stochastic RSI for energy and divergence, including the fast variant.
- A stack of EMAs (9, 50, 100, 200) for regime and gatekeeping.
- Ichimoku for the state of the market.
- Keltner channels and the Watson envelope for extremes and mean reversion.

Timeframes form a ladder. A lower-timeframe entry is only meaningful when it agrees with the story on the higher timeframe.

Sources: *The Basic of TA — Setting Up Charts* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY); *Lesson Number 5 — Stochastic RSI and Keltner Channels* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7MmCcxadAwQ); *How to Approach Timeframe* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VoIr0w6l8gc).

## 10. Bankroll and warnings

Start small, keep size constant, separate long-term holdings from trading capital, and withdraw profits. Every lesson returns to the same point: the edge is mostly behavioural. The trader who follows a modest plan consistently will do better than the trader with a brilliant setup and no rules.

Sources: *Becoming a Trader Part 2 — Bankroll Management* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0LFo5f1TtHA); *Introduction — New to This YouTube?* ([08:32], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JKLiG3p-qN4).

## Naked RSI, Stochastic RSI and the NKED Method
Source: https://trading-study-notes.sanliurfa.workers.dev/notes/D_stochastic

# Naked RSI, Stochastic RSI and the NKED Method

*Original reference notes. The linked videos are the original sources and remain their authors' property. Click a timestamp to verify any claim at its source.*

## 1. First principles

The method assumes the market is imperfect and heavily influenced by large participants. That is why it avoids precision: levels are zones, not exact numbers, and a reading is evidence about the state of the market rather than a signal that must be obeyed. Indicators are guides, not instructions.

The overall aim is to describe the *energy* behind a move — how much room is left, whether momentum is confirming price, and whether the higher timeframe supports the lower-timeframe story.

Sources: *How to NAKEDRSI* ([03:13], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bj8tpCSfjdI); *Stochastic RSI — Deeper Breakdown* ([01:57], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iOXOgQCX5f4); *NKED Method* ([10:07], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVHd_vf-KX8).

## 2. Settings and thresholds

### RSI ("naked RSI")

Use the default RSI. The moving-average baseline can be removed or kept; when kept, a cross above it is one signal among others. The health levels used throughout the material are **36, 46, 56 and 65**:

- **46–56** is the neutral range. Inside it, direction is close to a coin flip.
- **Above 56** adds bullish confirmation; moving back below 56 weakens that confirmation.
- **Below 46** starts to turn bearish.
- **36** is a soft bearish level — "somewhat" bearish rather than extreme. A break of 36 on a higher timeframe is treated as meaningful damage to the bull structure.
- **65** acts as a ceiling where pushes are often rejected, particularly when price has run far above it.
- Classic 70/30 extremes are acknowledged but treated as secondary. Historical examples cited include very low readings near 9–25 and highs near 87 or 95–99.

Sources: *How to NAKEDRSI* ([04:01], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bj8tpCSfjdI); ([06:02], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bj8tpCSfjdI); ([10:45], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bj8tpCSfjdI); ([26:11], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bj8tpCSfjdI); ([28:09], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bj8tpCSfjdI); *NKED Method* ([29:52], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVHd_vf-KX8); ([43:34], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVHd_vf-KX8).

### Stochastic RSI

Classic stochastic RSI is bounded between 0 and 100. The conventional 80/20 bands are noted, but the material explicitly downgrades them relative to RSI: stochastic RSI can stay oversold or overbought for a long time, so the label alone is a weak signal.

The **fast stochastic RSI** is a modified version with settings **3369**. Its stated purpose is to react sooner than the normal stochastic, and the comparison between fast and slow is used to judge whether a move is losing energy. A rejection zone around 40–60 is mentioned for the fast version.

Sources: *Lesson Number 5 — Stochastic RSI and Keltner Channels* ([01:57], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7MmCcxadAwQ); *NKED Method* ([17:08], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVHd_vf-KX8); ([18:12], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVHd_vf-KX8).

### EMAs, Ichimoku, Keltner and Watson

- **9 EMA** — short-term regime marker. Price below it suggests a weaker short-term picture.
- **50 EMA** — a level that strong bullish moves tend to respect.
- **100 EMA** — described as the trend gatekeeper across timeframes; holding above it is the main condition for an uptrend.
- **200 EMA** — the final structural line that major moves are expected to respect.
- **Ichimoku Cloud** — used to classify the state of the market: above the cloud is bullish, below is bearish, inside is turbulent.
- **Keltner channels** — default multiplier 1 on lower timeframes, around 2 on higher timeframes; the midline is used for rotation reads.
- **Watson envelope** — an outer band; the rule is that it should sit outside the Keltner. A green line entering the Keltner is treated as bearish, a red line entering it as bullish.

Sources: *NKED Method* ([22:59], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVHd_vf-KX8); *EMA Lesson Part 2* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oOcPYZSOCBw); *Ichimoku Cloud — How to Use* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L4tJI7bWrGc); *Watson Envelope + Keltner* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5hiv8vzMxcA); *Lesson Number 5* ([25:39], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7MmCcxadAwQ).

## 3. Reading RSI health

The 46–56 band defines the middle of the market. When price pushes above 56 and holds, the move has confirmation; when RSI slips back under 46, the burden of proof shifts to the bears. A reading at 36 is bearish but not hopeless, and a failure at 65 after a strong run is used as evidence of exhaustion.

The RSI trend line is drawn the same way as a price trend line. A break of that line is treated as a change in the character of the move, often earlier than the equivalent break on price.

Sources: *How to NAKEDRSI* ([06:02], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bj8tpCSfjdI); ([28:09], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bj8tpCSfjdI); *The Basic of TA — Setting Up Charts* ([50:02], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY).

## 4. Overbought and oversold as states

The single most important correction in the material is that an extreme reading is not a sell or buy signal. An overbought stochastic in a strong uptrend can stay overbought, and an oversold reading in a downtrend can stay oversold. The correct question is what *kind* of overbought or oversold it is — bullish overbought versus exhausted overbought, bearish oversold versus bouncy oversold.

Two practical rules are given. If stochastic RSI falls without ever reaching the oversold zone, that is read as strong bullish behaviour. If oscillators remain extended for roughly eight to ten candles, the probability of a reversal increases.

Sources: *Stochastic RSI — Deeper Breakdown* ([05:35], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iOXOgQCX5f4); ([10:52], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iOXOgQCX5f4); *Lesson Number 5* ([12:12], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7MmCcxadAwQ); *How to Approach Timeframe* ([08:07], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VoIr0w6l8gc).

## 5. Divergence

Divergence is a comparison between price and oscillator, not a standalone entry:

- Higher price with higher RSI is healthy.
- Higher price with lower RSI warns that the move is losing support.
- Lower price with higher RSI can mark bearish exhaustion.
- Rising successive stochastic bottoms while price holds or rises is bullish; successive lower highs in the oscillator while price rises is bearish.

A trend-change gate is emphasised: a bearish divergence is not acted on until price has returned to the overbought area and failed to make a significantly higher high. The worked example contrasts a stochastic top near 48k with RSI around 56 and a later top near 25k with RSI around 46.

Sources: *Stochastic RSI — Deeper Breakdown* ([02:31], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iOXOgQCX5f4); ([03:05], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iOXOgQCX5f4); ([14:55], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iOXOgQCX5f4); *Lesson Number 5* ([07:42], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7MmCcxadAwQ).

## 6. Multi-timeframe method

The timeframe ladder is built on three-minute, nine-minute and twenty-seven-minute candles, with the "times nine" rule used to translate a candle on one timeframe into roughly nine candles on the one below. Higher timeframes (daily, three-day, weekly, monthly) define the story; lower timeframes provide the entry.

The recommended learning order is to start high and work down. A trader who begins on the three-minute chart learns noise instead of context.

Sources: *How to Approach Timeframe* ([07:32], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VoIr0w6l8gc); *Stochastic RSI — Deeper Breakdown* ([07:45], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iOXOgQCX5f4); *Lesson Number 5* ([03:21], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7MmCcxadAwQ).

## 7. Keltner channels and the envelope

Keltner bands act as a magnet. Price that moves outside them tends to be pulled back toward the middle; in a strong bear move it may instead travel sideways in an L-shape until the bands catch up. Rotation is described as top → middle → bottom, with a break of the middle opening a move toward the opposite band.

The 9 EMA combined with the bands is used as a regime signal: a 9 EMA below the lower band on the weekly is read as strongly bearish; above the upper band as strongly bullish.

Sources: *Lesson Number 5* ([26:16], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7MmCcxadAwQ); ([27:21], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7MmCcxadAwQ); ([29:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7MmCcxadAwQ); ([34:58], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7MmCcxadAwQ); *NKED Method* ([56:05], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVHd_vf-KX8).

## 8. NKED method in steps

1. Classify the regime with Ichimoku and the higher-timeframe EMAs.
2. Read RSI health against 36 / 46 / 56 / 65.
3. Compare the fast stochastic (3369) with the slow one to gauge energy.
4. Check divergences against price and require a failed return to an extreme before acting.
5. Locate Keltner and Watson extremes for mean-reversion context.
6. Require volume confirmation on the instrument and on Bitcoin/Ethereum.
7. Drop to the lower timeframe only to time the entry inside the higher-timeframe story.
8. Place the stop at the structural invalidation level.
9. Take a partial close into strength and let the remainder ride with a wider stop.
10. Record the decision in the journal and review it against the original story.

Sources: *NKED Method* ([17:08], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVHd_vf-KX8); ([56:33], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVHd_vf-KX8); *Lesson Number 5* ([08:52], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7MmCcxadAwQ).

## 9. Failure modes

The named errors are: selling an overbought reading without regime context, treating the oscillator as a guarantee, ignoring the higher timeframe, drawing trend lines on stochastic RSI before gaining experience, extending stops when the story has not changed, and using indicators as a crutch rather than as one input among several.

Sources: *Stochastic RSI — Deeper Breakdown* ([10:52], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iOXOgQCX5f4); *Lesson Number 5* ([01:26], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7MmCcxadAwQ).

## Indicators and Chart Reading
Source: https://trading-study-notes.sanliurfa.workers.dev/notes/E_indicators

# Indicators and Chart Reading

*Original study notes. The linked videos are the original sources and remain their authors' property. Click a timestamp to verify a claim at its source.*

## 1. What technical analysis is for

Technical analysis is treated as a way of assigning probabilities, not as a way of knowing the future. The market can be read as close to a coin flip on any single trade; the edge comes from context, concentration, and consistent decision-making. Confidence and self-belief are prerequisites, because a trader who does not trust their own process will not follow it.

Sources: *The Basic of TA — Setting Up Charts* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY); ([35:09], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY).

## 2. Chart setup: levels and volume clusters

The first tool is the horizontal line. Draw lines at obvious highs and lows and extend them indefinitely into the future — a level does not stop mattering because it was drawn last month. Areas where a lot of volume changed hands are called "areas of battle": a zone where buyers and sellers repeatedly fought, and therefore a zone price is likely to revisit.

Volume bars at the bottom of the chart are part of the same read. A candle body moving through a low-volume area is weaker evidence than one moving through a high-volume area. Wick and body are read separately: a long wick into a level followed by a close back inside shows rejection.

Worked examples in the sources include the 3,900–3,970 area in ETH, the 4,000 level, and a first weekly close above 4,000 that opened a move toward 4,800. In BTC, a 1,928 line of best fit on the four-hour chart marked the break that the daily chart hid.

Sources: *The Basic of TA — Setting Up Charts* ([24:25], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY); ([28:54], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY); ([30:50], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY).

## 3. Trend lines and timeframes

Trend lines are drawn on price and on oscillators in the same way: connect the relevant sequence of highs or lows and watch for a break of the line. Multiple possible paths should be sketched rather than one forecast, so that the trader can react to whichever path price actually takes.

Lower timeframes show detail that daily candles hide. The four-hour chart may reveal a break of a line that looks intact on the daily. Conversely, the higher timeframe decides whether a lower-timeframe signal is worth acting on.

Sources: *The Basic of TA — Setting Up Charts* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY); *How to Approach Timeframe* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VoIr0w6l8gc).

## 4. RSI and stochastic RSI

Textbook RSI rules (above 50 bullish, above 70 overbought, below 30 oversold) are acknowledged but replaced in practice by the health levels 36 / 46 / 56 / 65 described in the dedicated indicator note. Selling a reading simply because it is oversold is specifically discouraged, because oversold can stay oversold.

Stochastic RSI oscillates between 0 and 100 with conventional 80/20 bands. The more useful read is divergence: a stochastic at 100 while RSI has only reached the high 30s or low 30s indicates a weak move. Trend lines drawn on RSI are treated like price trend lines, and a break of the RSI line can precede the price break.

Sources: *The Basic of TA — Setting Up Charts* ([46:19], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY); ([47:21], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY); ([50:02], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY); *How to NAKEDRSI* ([04:01], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bj8tpCSfjdI).

## 5. The EMA stack

- **9 EMA** — the fastest regime marker. Used as the short-term trend setter and in combinations with Keltner bands.
- **30 and 50 EMA** — described as close companions and gatekeepers in bullish moves; the 50 often provides the bounce in a strong trend.
- **100 EMA** — the main trend gatekeeper. As long as price holds above it, the broader uptrend is considered intact.
- **200 EMA** — the final structural line; failure here changes the character of the move.

EMA crossings are covered in a separate lesson. The emphasis in these notes is on price relative to a level as a regime filter, rather than on any single crossover as a mechanical signal.

Sources: *Basic Explanation of EMAs Part 1* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1mO0lB8X8nc); *EMA Lesson Part 2 — Crossing EMAs* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oOcPYZSOCBw); *NKED Method* ([22:59], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVHd_vf-KX8).

## 6. Ichimoku and the Keltner/Watson layer

Ichimoku provides the market state: price above the cloud is a bullish environment, below it a bearish one, and inside it a volatile environment where direction is unresolved. The cloud is also described in energy terms — a zone whose boundaries matter for where momentum gathers.

Keltner channels supply mean-reversion context. Price outside the bands is usually pulled back toward the middle, though a strong trend may move sideways until the bands catch up. The Watson envelope sits outside the Keltner; a green line entering the Keltner is bearish, a red line entering it bullish.

Sources: *Ichimoku Cloud — How to Use* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L4tJI7bWrGc); *Watson Envelope + Keltner* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5hiv8vzMxcA); *Lesson Number 5* ([29:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7MmCcxadAwQ).

## 7. Combining the indicators

The indicators are not independent signals. A single story is assembled: regime from Ichimoku and EMAs, health from RSI, energy from fast and slow stochastic, extremes from Keltner and Watson, and confirmation from volume. A lower-timeframe entry is only taken when it agrees with that story.

Sources: *How to Approach Timeframe* ([07:32], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VoIr0w6l8gc); *NKED Method* ([17:08], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVHd_vf-KX8).

## 8. Warnings

Keep a separate long-term portfolio and a small trading portfolio. Do not use high leverage without understanding the sizing implications. Training takes months, and a trader exposed to only one market regime will be unprepared when conditions change. Bitcoin dominance is background context: when Bitcoin turns down, most altcoins follow.

Sources: *The Basic of TA — Setting Up Charts* ([29:56], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY); ([38:36], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zv8pXI_7VJY); *Introduction — New to This YouTube?* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JKLiG3p-qN4).

## Volume, Order Flow and Timing
Source: https://trading-study-notes.sanliurfa.workers.dev/notes/F_volume_timing

# Volume, Order Flow and Timing

*Original study notes. The linked videos are the original sources and remain their authors' property. Click a timestamp to verify a claim at its source.*

## 1. Volume as the primary evidence

The material treats volume as more reliable than chart narratives: price levels matter, but the size of the participation at those levels determines whether a move is real. Technical analysis is framed as betting analysis, not prediction.

Order-flow data has to be observed continuously. A short visit once or twice a day misses the accumulation that matters. The setup described uses a dedicated machine or virtual private server running the tool for long stretches, and the suggested quote currency is USD rather than USDT.

Sources: *How to Use Aggr.Trade — Volume to Predict the Market* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EO6nFd5-Fl0); *How to Approach Timeframe* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VoIr0w6l8gc).

## 2. Thresholds

The 2024 setup uses a rolling fifteen-minute window — a continuous fifteen minutes of trading, not a fifteen-minute candle. The 2025 update raises the numbers:

- roughly **50 million in five minutes** is the minimum for meaningful activity;
- roughly **300 million in fifteen minutes** indicates good activity;
- one side exceeding the other by more than **300 million** indicates clear directional pressure;
- breaking a major resistance can require close to **a billion** in aggressive shorts, for example near ETH 4,250 or BTC 107.2.

These are reference figures from the source videos, not universal constants; they are repeated here so the timestamp links can be used to check the context.

Sources: *How to Use Aggr.Trade* ([02:17], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EO6nFd5-Fl0); *How to Use Aggr.Trade — 2025 Update* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KPD2ElzbQnc).

## 3. Delta and fake moves

The tape shows the battle between aggressive buyers and sellers. When shorts keep piling up while longs also build, the move is contested; a rapid change in the ratio — such as a reading dropping from the low hundreds to around seventy — is used as a signal to take profit.

Absorption matters: if large volume hits a level without price moving, the level is being defended. Liquidation hunts push price through obvious clusters of stops before the move resumes.

Sources: *How to Use Aggr.Trade* ([11:56], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EO6nFd5-Fl0); ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EO6nFd5-Fl0).

## 4. Order books are a trap

The source material warns against using the order book as a primary signal: visible liquidity is often moved or spoofed, and traders who rely on it tend to be stopped out. The advice is to use executed volume and delta instead.

Sources: *How to Use Aggr.Trade* ([05:42], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EO6nFd5-Fl0).

## 5. Altcoins lead; ETH joins Bitcoin

Smaller coins are described as leading indicators: they tend to dump before Bitcoin and to sell off first when risk appetite changes. The 2025 update adds that volume leadership shifted toward Ethereum, so both BTC and ETH are checked before a timing decision.

Sources: *How to Use Aggr.Trade — 2025 Update* ([02:08], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KPD2ElzbQnc); *How to Use Aggr.Trade* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EO6nFd5-Fl0).

## 6. Worked examples

A January 2024 BTC short around 40.4k/40.2k is used to show taking profit when the aggressive-volume ratio collapsed. A 2025 example marks the bottom of the Keltner/Watson area near 4,306 on the twenty-seven-minute chart and notes that a reversal would need a volume increase on both Bitcoin and Ethereum.

Sources: *How to Use Aggr.Trade* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EO6nFd5-Fl0); *How to Use Aggr.Trade — 2025 Update* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KPD2ElzbQnc).

## 7. Timeframe theory

The ladder is built on 3, 6 and 9, with the "times nine" rule connecting a candle to the timeframe above or below it (three three-minute candles make a nine-minute candle; three nine-minute candles make a twenty-seven-minute candle). The proposed translation factor between a timeframe and the next is roughly nine to twelve candles.

Practical guidance is to start on higher timeframes and work down. A lower-timeframe signal is only an entry mechanism for a story already established above it.

Sources: *How to Approach Timeframe* ([07:32], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VoIr0w6l8gc); *Stochastic RSI — Deeper Breakdown* ([07:45], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iOXOgQCX5f4).

## 8. Writing the story

Before entering, write down: the goal for the trade, the side, the timeframe, the higher-timeframe context, the invalidation level, and the volume condition that would confirm or deny the idea. The oscillator's role is to describe energy — a fast stochastic can stay extended for around eight or nine candles, so extension alone is not a reversal signal.

Sources: *How to Approach Timeframe* ([08:07], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VoIr0w6l8gc); *Part 1 — Timing Your Positions* ([04:48], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NyGIkmMb-Sw).

## 9. Timing entries and exits

A good entry is close to a structural level with room to place the stop beyond the noise. The material gives an example of a long near 3,292 with an invalidation near 3,381 and notes that an instrument like ETH can often be re-entered within a narrow price range, so waiting for the right tick is practical.

Profit-taking is planned at the same time: close part of the position into strength and give the remainder a wider stop. Focus on one coin — the first step toward better timing is knowing one instrument well rather than watching ten.

Sources: *Part 1 — Timing Your Positions* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NyGIkmMb-Sw); *Lesson 2 — Alpha That Will Save You Thousands* ([28:41], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rLdY77E8KzA); *Key Thoughts Going Into 2026* ([00:00], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ti3JhXEY9UM).

## 10. Practice loop

Timing improves through experience, a journal, and controlled size. Record the reason for each entry and exit, review the outcome against the original story, and change one thing at a time.

Sources: *Lesson 1 — Introduction to Trading* ([13:34], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LKJPwG14y2M); *The Key to Success* ([18:08], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UfxEboq-tOM).

# Trading Study Notes

A free, self-contained study guide built from public trading lessons. It is written in original prose and released into the public domain — see [License](license.md) and [Attribution & scope](notice.md).

## How to use this site

- Every **highlighted timestamp** opens the original video at that exact moment, so any claim here can be checked against its source.
- Plain video URLs are clickable and open in a new tab.
- The pages are static HTML. No account, tracking, or internet connection is needed to read the text.

## Contents

1. [Foundations — mindset, bankroll and journaling](notes/A_foundations.md) — the core premise, starting small, self-data, sizing, withdrawals, rules and the learning routine.
2. [Mistakes and risk](notes/B_mistakes.md) — failure patterns, profit retention, stop-loss philosophy, liquidity, overtrading and toolkit discipline.
3. [Lessons and philosophy](notes/C_lessons.md) — the game metaphor, sources of edge, happy decisions, leverage, shorting and the chart toolkit.
4. [Naked RSI, stochastic RSI and NKED](notes/D_stochastic.md) — exact levels and settings, divergence, multi-timeframe method and a step-by-step workflow.
5. [Indicators and chart reading](notes/E_indicators.md) — levels and volume clusters, EMAs, Ichimoku, Keltner/Watson and how the tools combine.
6. [Volume, order flow and timing](notes/F_volume_timing.md) — volume thresholds, delta, order-book traps, timeframe theory and entry timing.
